top_news.title: Immuna Therapeutics AG and NIMS University Rajasthan Announce US$3 Million Partnership to Expand Access to Advanced CAR-T Cancer Therapy in India
top_news.summary: VMPL Berlin [Germany], October 14: Immuna Therapeutics AG, based in Allschwil, Basel region, Switzerland, and NIMS University Rajasthan, Jaipur, today announced a US3millionpartnershiptodevelopanaffordable,locallydeliveredmodelforCAR-TcelltherapyinRajasthan.AnnouncedattheWorldHealthSummitinBerlin,thecollaborationaimstoestablishaRajasthanCentreofExcellenceforCAR-Tclinicaldelivery,researchandtraining.NIMSwouldcontributeUS2 million towards infrastructure, clinical operations and patient care, while Immuna would contribute US$1 million in technology, training and technical implementation. The partnership is intended to create a scalable model that could extend access to advanced cancer treatments beyond major metropolitan centres. A breakthrough in cancer care , but access remains a challenge Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy represents a major advance in cancer treatment. It involves collecting a patient's T cells, genetically engineering them to recognise and attack cancer cells, and returning the modified cells to the patient. In certain blood cancers, including some leukemias and lymphomas, CAR-T therapy has produced deep and sometimes long-lasting remissions, including in patients whose disease has returned or failed to respond to other treatments. Yet complex manufacturing, specialised infrastructure, clinical monitoring and high treatment costs have limited access in many countries. The challenge is no longer simply to develop transformative therapies, but to build safe, sustainable delivery models that can make them accessible to more patients Immuna's approach: advanced TriCAR technology with local delivery. Immuna is developing an alternative model built around local clinical capacity, technology transfer and a more affordable treatment package. The collaboration would provide technical processes to NIMS, supported by training, standard operating procedures, quality and process implementation, and regulatory technical support. The longer-term ambition is to bring qualified treatment and, where approved, manufacturing capacity closer to patients, reducing dependence on centralised delivery models. The proposed patient-package price is capped at INR 30 lakh. Prof. (Dr.) Balvir S. Tomar, Founder and Chancellor of NIMS University Rajasthan, said: India has the scientific talent, clinical expertise and entrepreneurial capacity to help reshape how advanced cancer treatments are delivered. Our partnership with Immuna is an opportunity to build that capacity in Rajasthan, combining world-class technology with local infrastructure and clinical expertise. Our ambition is to develop a model in which geography and economic circumstances do not automatically determine whether a patient can access the next generation of cancer care. Dr Boro Dropuli a pioneer in lentiviral-vector technology and a member of Immuna's technical leadership, said: The promise of cell and gene therapy depends not only on the science, but on our ability to translate that science into reliable, reproducible and accessible treatments. TriCAR-T brings together multi-target recognition and a delivery model designed with affordability and technology transfer in mind. Building local capabilities, supported by robust quality systems and regulatory oversight, is an important step towards making these advanced therapies available to more patients. Pradeep Kakkattil, Co-founder of Immuna Therapeutics and Founder and CEO of Health Innovation Exchange, said: We cannot accept a future in which the most advanced cancer therapies are available only to people who can afford treatment abroad or in a handful of specialist centres. Immuna is building a model that combines advanced gene therapy with local delivery, technology transfer and a more affordable price point. Our work with NIMS in Rajasthan is part of a broader effort to work with states, hospitals and partners globally to expand access to novel gene therapies for cancer and, over time, other diseases, including autoimmune conditions. The ambition is to move from isolated centres of excellence to a network of local capabilities that can reach more patients Prof. Sanjay Pattanshetty, NIMS University Rajasthan, said: Expanding access to advanced cancer care requires us to bring together clinical excellence, research, technology and a commitment to affordability. Our collaboration with Immuna offers an opportunity to build these capabilities in Rajasthan, while training healthcare professionals and developing a model that can serve patients across the state and beyond. We look forward to helping establish a strong foundation for the responsible introduction of next-generation cell and gene therapies in India. A significant opportunity for Rajasthan and India Rajasthan, with an estimated population of approximately 8.4 crore in 2026, offers an opportunity to establish a regional hub for advanced cellular therapies. The partnership's planning estimates indicate: - 90,000-100,000: estimated new cancer cases of all types annually in Rajasthan. - 2,200-2,700: estimated annual cases of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and selected chronic lymphocytic leukemia potentially relevant to the programme's target antigens. The proposed model would combine a Jaipur-based clinical hub with patient identification and referrals across Rajasthan. The partners intend to explore pathways involving government health programmes, insurers, corporate social responsibility funding and other hospitals to improve access. Building a wider network for advanced therapies The Rajasthan initiative is part of Immuna's broader ambition to expand access to advanced cellular and gene therapies through partnerships with state governments, academic institutions, hospitals and international collaborators. Immuna is working to develop models that combine technology transfer, local clinical capacity, quality systems and innovative financing, with the longer-term goal of extending these approaches to other blood malignancies and selected autoimmune diseases as the relevant technologies and clinical evidence mature. For India, the partnership offers an opportunity to build expertise in advanced therapy delivery and potentially develop a model that can be adapted in other states. Internationally, it reflects a growing effort to ensure that advances in cell and gene therapy are accompanied by practical approaches to affordability, local capability and equitable access. About Immuna Therapeutics Immuna Therapeutics AG is a Switzerland-based biotechnology venture focused on transforming access to cancer care through advanced cell and gene therapies. Its ambition is to develop more affordable and decentralised approaches to delivering innovative treatments, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, through technology transfer and partnerships with local institutions. About NIMS University Rajasthan NIMS University Rajasthan, Jaipur, is a higher-education and healthcare institution with clinical and academic capabilities. Through this proposed collaboration, NIMS aims to develop its role in advanced cancer care, clinical research and the delivery of innovative therapies in Rajasthan. top_news.title: Libya: Eastern Authorities Carry Out Wave of Executions
top_news.summary: Click to expand Image Military leader of Eastern Libya, Khalifa Haftar (center), attends a conference in Sabha, Libya, September 5, 2024. 2024 Khaled Nasraoui/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Photo (Beirut) - The Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), which controls eastern and southernLibya, has executed at least 31 people since late August 2026 following grossly unfair military trials, Human Rights Watch said today. These are the first known executions in Libya since 2010, with at least 50 more people in Gernada military prison at imminentrisk of execution. On August 23, the LAAF military prosecutorannounced that 10 people had been executed by firing squad after being convicted of murder and terrorism-related offenses. Human rights groups havedocumented a total of at least 31 executions as of September 10. The LAAF, led by General Khalifa Haftar, should immediately halt all executions and impose a moratorium on the death penalty, Human Rights Watch said. "The Libyan Arab Armed Forces are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya's own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians," saidBassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. "Every execution carried out under these conditions is an irreversible injustice and every government with influence over the LAAF should be pressing hard to stop the next one." Many of those executed had been arrested in the cities of Derna and Benghazi during or after thearmed conflict between the LAAF and opposing armed groups between 2014 and 2018. Between 2018 and 2021, military courts in eastern Libyaconvicted hundreds of civilians in secret trials targeting real or perceived critics of the LAAF, sentencing at least 22 to death. According to Amnesty International, many of the sentences were based on confessions allegedly extracted under torture by the Internal Security Agency, an LAAF-affiliated armed group. At least two death sentences werereduced to life in prison on appeal by a higher military court in 2019, yet the defendants were put to death this year regardless. The executions also went ahead despite a November 2025ruling by the constitutional chamber of Libya's Supreme Court that Law No. 4/2017 is unconstitutional insofar as it grants military courts jurisdiction to try civilians for terrorism and crimes against the state. Local human rights groups said that the military trials violated defendants' due process rights. They wereheld in secret and without prior notice. Defendants' families, journalists, and human rights organizations were not allowed to attend. Severaldefendants were denied lawyers of their choice and those who did have their own lawyers were refused visits before and during trial and could not speak with them privately. They were apparentlynot allowed to present their cases in court or examine the evidence against them. The verdicts were handed down without providing the defendants or their attorneys with written and reasoned judgments. Trying civilians in military courts is incompatible with the right toa fair trial under human rights law and such trials violate the right to be tried before an independent and impartial tribunal. In Libya, military prosecutors are often not qualified to investigate civilians and they lack independence. The military prosecutors and judges in eastern Libya are themselves affiliated with the LAAF or allied armed groups. Families of defendants were not notified in advance that the executions would take place. The authorities refused to hand over the bodies of those executed, asked relatives to confirm the identities of the dead, then buried them without families present and warned relatives not to hold funerals. Secret executions and denying families a last visit violate international law, including by inflictingsevere mental suffering on those executed and their relatives inbreach of the absolute prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. Libya remains split between two rival authorities. The Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU), which is internationally recognized, controls the west, alongside affiliated security agencies and armed groups. The LAAF and affiliated forces and militias control the east and south. Both sides operate with near-total impunity. TheUnited Nations and theGNU condemned the executions. Governments that fund, train, and legitimize the LAAF have real leverage, and a responsibility to use it, publicly and privately, to press LAAF leaders to halt all executions, Human Rights Watch said. Libya's justice sector is fragmented and deeply polarized. Human Rights Watch has previouslydocumented outdated and repressive legislation, a lack of fair trial rights, and rampant due process violations. Unaccountable militias control prisons that are only nominally under state ministries. Libyan authorities in both the east and west should restrict the jurisdiction of military courts to military offenses committed by military personnel and stop trying civilians in military courts altogether. They should promptly review all cases of civilians wrongfully detained and prosecuted before military courts and provide effective remedies, including release, transfer to civilian courts, or retrial in line with international fair trial standards, with acknowledgment of time served. Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all countries and under all circumstances because it is inherently inhumane, uniquely cruel and irreversible, and universally plagued by arbitrariness, prejudice, and error. Ninety-two countries haveratified a protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights that requires the abolition of the death penalty, recognizing that capital punishment violates the right to life and the prohibition of cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment. Libya should abolish the death penalty and until then enact a moratorium on all executions. "Libya went more than 15 years without an execution, and the LAAF has shattered that moratorium in a matter of weeks," Khawaja said. "The lives of at least 50 more people now depend on whether Haftar's forces, and the governments that back them, choose to stop this."

articles.title: Immuna Therapeutics AG and NIMS University Rajasthan Announce US$3 Million Partnership to Expand Access to Advanced CAR-T Cancer Therapy in India
articles.summary: VMPL Berlin [Germany], October 14: Immuna Therapeutics AG, based in Allschwil, Basel region, Switzerland, and NIMS University Rajasthan, Jaipur, today announced a US3millionpartnershiptodevelopanaffordable,locallydeliveredmodelforCAR-TcelltherapyinRajasthan.AnnouncedattheWorldHealthSummitinBerlin,thecollaborationaimstoestablishaRajasthanCentreofExcellenceforCAR-Tclinicaldelivery,researchandtraining.NIMSwouldcontributeUS2 million towards infrastructure, clinical operations and patient care, while Immuna would contribute US$1 million in technology, training and technical implementation. The partnership is intended to create a scalable model that could extend access to advanced cancer treatments beyond major metropolitan centres. A breakthrough in cancer care , but access remains a challenge Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy represents a major advance in cancer treatment. It involves collecting a patient's T cells, genetically engineering them to recognise and attack cancer cells, and returning the modified cells to the patient. In certain blood cancers, including some leukemias and lymphomas, CAR-T therapy has produced deep and sometimes long-lasting remissions, including in patients whose disease has returned or failed to respond to other treatments. Yet complex manufacturing, specialised infrastructure, clinical monitoring and high treatment costs have limited access in many countries. The challenge is no longer simply to develop transformative therapies, but to build safe, sustainable delivery models that can make them accessible to more patients Immuna's approach: advanced TriCAR technology with local delivery. Immuna is developing an alternative model built around local clinical capacity, technology transfer and a more affordable treatment package. The collaboration would provide technical processes to NIMS, supported by training, standard operating procedures, quality and process implementation, and regulatory technical support. The longer-term ambition is to bring qualified treatment and, where approved, manufacturing capacity closer to patients, reducing dependence on centralised delivery models. The proposed patient-package price is capped at INR 30 lakh. Prof. (Dr.) Balvir S. Tomar, Founder and Chancellor of NIMS University Rajasthan, said: India has the scientific talent, clinical expertise and entrepreneurial capacity to help reshape how advanced cancer treatments are delivered. Our partnership with Immuna is an opportunity to build that capacity in Rajasthan, combining world-class technology with local infrastructure and clinical expertise. Our ambition is to develop a model in which geography and economic circumstances do not automatically determine whether a patient can access the next generation of cancer care. Dr Boro Dropuli a pioneer in lentiviral-vector technology and a member of Immuna's technical leadership, said: The promise of cell and gene therapy depends not only on the science, but on our ability to translate that science into reliable, reproducible and accessible treatments. TriCAR-T brings together multi-target recognition and a delivery model designed with affordability and technology transfer in mind. Building local capabilities, supported by robust quality systems and regulatory oversight, is an important step towards making these advanced therapies available to more patients. Pradeep Kakkattil, Co-founder of Immuna Therapeutics and Founder and CEO of Health Innovation Exchange, said: We cannot accept a future in which the most advanced cancer therapies are available only to people who can afford treatment abroad or in a handful of specialist centres. Immuna is building a model that combines advanced gene therapy with local delivery, technology transfer and a more affordable price point. Our work with NIMS in Rajasthan is part of a broader effort to work with states, hospitals and partners globally to expand access to novel gene therapies for cancer and, over time, other diseases, including autoimmune conditions. The ambition is to move from isolated centres of excellence to a network of local capabilities that can reach more patients Prof. Sanjay Pattanshetty, NIMS University Rajasthan, said: Expanding access to advanced cancer care requires us to bring together clinical excellence, research, technology and a commitment to affordability. Our collaboration with Immuna offers an opportunity to build these capabilities in Rajasthan, while training healthcare professionals and developing a model that can serve patients across the state and beyond. We look forward to helping establish a strong foundation for the responsible introduction of next-generation cell and gene therapies in India. A significant opportunity for Rajasthan and India Rajasthan, with an estimated population of approximately 8.4 crore in 2026, offers an opportunity to establish a regional hub for advanced cellular therapies. The partnership's planning estimates indicate: - 90,000-100,000: estimated new cancer cases of all types annually in Rajasthan. - 2,200-2,700: estimated annual cases of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and selected chronic lymphocytic leukemia potentially relevant to the programme's target antigens. The proposed model would combine a Jaipur-based clinical hub with patient identification and referrals across Rajasthan. The partners intend to explore pathways involving government health programmes, insurers, corporate social responsibility funding and other hospitals to improve access. Building a wider network for advanced therapies The Rajasthan initiative is part of Immuna's broader ambition to expand access to advanced cellular and gene therapies through partnerships with state governments, academic institutions, hospitals and international collaborators. Immuna is working to develop models that combine technology transfer, local clinical capacity, quality systems and innovative financing, with the longer-term goal of extending these approaches to other blood malignancies and selected autoimmune diseases as the relevant technologies and clinical evidence mature. For India, the partnership offers an opportunity to build expertise in advanced therapy delivery and potentially develop a model that can be adapted in other states. Internationally, it reflects a growing effort to ensure that advances in cell and gene therapy are accompanied by practical approaches to affordability, local capability and equitable access. About Immuna Therapeutics Immuna Therapeutics AG is a Switzerland-based biotechnology venture focused on transforming access to cancer care through advanced cell and gene therapies. Its ambition is to develop more affordable and decentralised approaches to delivering innovative treatments, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, through technology transfer and partnerships with local institutions. About NIMS University Rajasthan NIMS University Rajasthan, Jaipur, is a higher-education and healthcare institution with clinical and academic capabilities. Through this proposed collaboration, NIMS aims to develop its role in advanced cancer care, clinical research and the delivery of innovative therapies in Rajasthan. articles.title: Libya: Eastern Authorities Carry Out Wave of Executions
articles.summary: Click to expand Image Military leader of Eastern Libya, Khalifa Haftar (center), attends a conference in Sabha, Libya, September 5, 2024. 2024 Khaled Nasraoui/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Photo (Beirut) - The Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), which controls eastern and southernLibya, has executed at least 31 people since late August 2026 following grossly unfair military trials, Human Rights Watch said today. These are the first known executions in Libya since 2010, with at least 50 more people in Gernada military prison at imminentrisk of execution. On August 23, the LAAF military prosecutorannounced that 10 people had been executed by firing squad after being convicted of murder and terrorism-related offenses. Human rights groups havedocumented a total of at least 31 executions as of September 10. The LAAF, led by General Khalifa Haftar, should immediately halt all executions and impose a moratorium on the death penalty, Human Rights Watch said. "The Libyan Arab Armed Forces are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya's own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians," saidBassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. "Every execution carried out under these conditions is an irreversible injustice and every government with influence over the LAAF should be pressing hard to stop the next one." Many of those executed had been arrested in the cities of Derna and Benghazi during or after thearmed conflict between the LAAF and opposing armed groups between 2014 and 2018. Between 2018 and 2021, military courts in eastern Libyaconvicted hundreds of civilians in secret trials targeting real or perceived critics of the LAAF, sentencing at least 22 to death. According to Amnesty International, many of the sentences were based on confessions allegedly extracted under torture by the Internal Security Agency, an LAAF-affiliated armed group. At least two death sentences werereduced to life in prison on appeal by a higher military court in 2019, yet the defendants were put to death this year regardless. The executions also went ahead despite a November 2025ruling by the constitutional chamber of Libya's Supreme Court that Law No. 4/2017 is unconstitutional insofar as it grants military courts jurisdiction to try civilians for terrorism and crimes against the state. Local human rights groups said that the military trials violated defendants' due process rights. They wereheld in secret and without prior notice. Defendants' families, journalists, and human rights organizations were not allowed to attend. Severaldefendants were denied lawyers of their choice and those who did have their own lawyers were refused visits before and during trial and could not speak with them privately. They were apparentlynot allowed to present their cases in court or examine the evidence against them. The verdicts were handed down without providing the defendants or their attorneys with written and reasoned judgments. Trying civilians in military courts is incompatible with the right toa fair trial under human rights law and such trials violate the right to be tried before an independent and impartial tribunal. In Libya, military prosecutors are often not qualified to investigate civilians and they lack independence. The military prosecutors and judges in eastern Libya are themselves affiliated with the LAAF or allied armed groups. Families of defendants were not notified in advance that the executions would take place. The authorities refused to hand over the bodies of those executed, asked relatives to confirm the identities of the dead, then buried them without families present and warned relatives not to hold funerals. Secret executions and denying families a last visit violate international law, including by inflictingsevere mental suffering on those executed and their relatives inbreach of the absolute prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. Libya remains split between two rival authorities. The Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU), which is internationally recognized, controls the west, alongside affiliated security agencies and armed groups. The LAAF and affiliated forces and militias control the east and south. Both sides operate with near-total impunity. TheUnited Nations and theGNU condemned the executions. Governments that fund, train, and legitimize the LAAF have real leverage, and a responsibility to use it, publicly and privately, to press LAAF leaders to halt all executions, Human Rights Watch said. Libya's justice sector is fragmented and deeply polarized. Human Rights Watch has previouslydocumented outdated and repressive legislation, a lack of fair trial rights, and rampant due process violations. Unaccountable militias control prisons that are only nominally under state ministries. Libyan authorities in both the east and west should restrict the jurisdiction of military courts to military offenses committed by military personnel and stop trying civilians in military courts altogether. They should promptly review all cases of civilians wrongfully detained and prosecuted before military courts and provide effective remedies, including release, transfer to civilian courts, or retrial in line with international fair trial standards, with acknowledgment of time served. Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all countries and under all circumstances because it is inherently inhumane, uniquely cruel and irreversible, and universally plagued by arbitrariness, prejudice, and error. Ninety-two countries haveratified a protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights that requires the abolition of the death penalty, recognizing that capital punishment violates the right to life and the prohibition of cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment. Libya should abolish the death penalty and until then enact a moratorium on all executions. "Libya went more than 15 years without an execution, and the LAAF has shattered that moratorium in a matter of weeks," Khawaja said. "The lives of at least 50 more people now depend on whether Haftar's forces, and the governments that back them, choose to stop this."
